claims.statement: In its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee briefing on five CJC-1295 variants (CJC-1295 free base, CJC-1295 acetate, CJC-1295 DAC free base, CJC-1295 DAC acetate, CJC-1295 DAC TFA), FDA concluded the evaluation criteria weigh against placing any of them on the 503A Bulks List, citing immunogenicity risk (particularly for subcutaneous administration), pituitary DNA damage in genotoxicity testing, aggregation sensitivity, repeat-dose toxicity findings, and insufficient publicly available physical/chemical characterization data.

context.formulation: CJC-1295 free base, acetate, and DAC salt forms

claims.statement: CJC-1295 appears on FDA's public bulk-drug-substances page under "Bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn," not in the active Category 1 or Category 2 lists; the entry states FDA identified serious adverse events associated with CJC-1295 including increased heart rate and systemic vasodilatory reaction, and that available clinical data are limited. Prior to its current withdrawn-nomination status, CJC-1295 had been placed, in September 2023, into FDA's separate interim-policy "Category 2" list along with over a dozen other peptides; that Category 2 placement (of CJC-1295 alongside AOD-9604, ipamorelin acetate, and Thymosin Alpha-1) was the subject of an Administrative Procedure Act lawsuit against FDA brought by Evexias and Farmakeio.

claims.statement: CJC-1295 (including the DAC-conjugated form) is a synthetic peptide analog of human growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH 1-29) that activates GHRH receptors on anterior pituitary somatotroph cells to stimulate growth hormone release; the DAC (Drug Affinity Complex) modification is intended to extend plasma half-life via covalent albumin binding.

extractedEvidence.quote: CJC-1295 DAC...is a synthetic peptide analogue of the human GHRH1-29
The estimated half-life of CJC-1295 was 5.8-8.1 d.

claims.statement: In two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, ascending-dose trials (28-day and 49-day) in healthy adults ages 21-61, subcutaneous CJC-1295 produced dose-dependent increases in plasma GH (2- to 10-fold) lasting 6 or more days and IGF-I (1.5- to 3-fold) lasting 9-11 days after single doses; after multiple weekly or biweekly doses, mean IGF-I remained above baseline for up to 28 days, and no serious adverse reactions were reported in this supervised trial setting. The trials measured hormone-axis pharmacodynamics only; they did not assess body composition, strength, fat loss, sleep, or other downstream outcomes.

context.useCase: GH/IGF-I axis stimulation (investigational, pharmacodynamic endpoints only)
context.doseText: single ascending doses, and two-to-three weekly or biweekly doses, over 28- and 49-day trial protocols (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: Two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, ascending dose trials with durations of 28 and 49 d.
dose-dependent increases in mean plasma GH concentrations by 2- to 10-fold for 6 d or more and in mean plasma IGF-I concentrations by 1.5- to 3-fold for 9-11 d
No serious adverse reactions were reported.

reviewFlags: trial dose context must never be presented as a use recommendation

this trial predates and is independent of the CJC-1295 DAC phase 2 trial subject death reported in 2006 (see safety-critical claim below); does not establish long-term or self-administered gray-market safety

independent 2009 published study (PMID 19386527) replicates the direction of GH/IGF-1 axis activation, supporting that the pharmacodynamic finding is not a single-trial artifact; the precise dose-response magnitudes (2-10x GH, 1.5-3x IGF-I) and duration windows remain sourced only to the single Teichman 2006 RCT

claims.statement: FDA's briefing document states that ConjuChem Biotechnology withdrew CJC-1295 DAC from clinical trials in 2006 following the death of a subject involved in a phase 2 trial; nonclinical toxicology work also found DNA damage in pituitary cells (Comet assay) and repeat-dose findings including decreased activity, emesis, and injection-site inflammation, hemorrhage, and necrosis in animal studies.

context.population: phase 2 clinical trial subject (human); repeat-dose toxicology in animal studies

No independent primary source confirming or ruling out causal attribution was found this session; this claim and conflict cjc1295-conflict-cause-of-death-attribution-001 remain human-review-gated as instructed

claims.statement: "CJC-1295" refers to two distinct products sold under overlapping branding: CJC-1295 DAC (the long-acting, Drug Affinity Complex-conjugated form with a multi-day half-life, the subject of the withdrawn ConjuChem phase 2 program) and CJC-1295 without DAC (also marketed as Mod GRF 1-29), a shorter-acting GHRH(1-29) analog lacking the DAC modification; PubChem's structured record for CJC-1295 lists molecular formula C165H269N47O46 under CID 91971820.

reviewFlags: resolved on independent re-check (2026-08-29): PubChem holds a SEPARATE compound record, CID 91976842, explicitly named "CJC1295 Without DAC" (formula C152H252N44O42), distinct from the CID 91971820 record cited above -- this confirms PubChem does unambiguously distinguish DAC vs. non-DAC forms across two separate CIDs, resolving the prior gap

CAS number and UNII for PubChem CID 91971820 remain unresolved: an independent lookup via the FDA/NCATS Global Substance Registration System (GSRS) for "CJC-1295" returned 8 substance records (multiple UNII/CAS pairs for salt and related forms) and one clearer exact-name match (UNII 62RC32V9N7, CAS 446262-90-4) whose reported molecular formula did not cleanly match either PubChem CID's formula, so it could not be confidently attributed to CID 91971820 specifically; this identifier gap stays open for a reviewer with direct database/API access
vendor product listings for 'CJC-1295 without DAC' and 'Mod GRF 1-29' are not consistently distinguished from CJC-1295 DAC in gray-market marketing; this ambiguity itself is a consumer-facing risk

claims.statement: No approved CJC-1295 product exists, and the only published controlled human data measure GH/IGF-I pharmacodynamics in healthy adults over 28-49 days; that data does not establish the anti-aging, fat-loss, muscle-gain, sleep-quality, bone-density, or tissue-recovery benefits for which CJC-1295 is commonly marketed online (often stacked with ipamorelin). A vendor marketing page reviewed for this packet cited only the Teichman (2006) GH/IGF-I pharmacodynamic study and a separate pulsatility study as its human evidence, while asserting benefits for sleep architecture, bone density, lipolysis, lean mass, and tissue repair that those studies did not test.

context.formulation: research-grade CJC-1295, often combined with ipamorelin
context.useCase: anti-aging / body composition / sleep / recovery marketing claims

Enhanced deep sleep quality — GH secretion is coupled to slow-wave sleep architecture

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: popular marketing claims (sleep, bone density, lipolysis, lean mass, tissue repair) are mechanistic extrapolations from GH/IGF-I elevation, not clinically demonstrated human outcomes
capture parallel ipamorelin combination claims in the ipamorelin packet as well

conflicts.summary: FDA's PCAC briefing document states a phase 2 trial subject death led to ConjuChem's 2006 withdrawal of CJC-1295 DAC from clinical trials, but the fetched briefing text does not specify whether the death was causally attributed to the study drug. A targeted independent-review attempt (2026-08-29) located the matching ConjuChem Phase 2 trial on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00267527, terminated September 2006) but its public record states no termination reason or cause-of-death detail, and a PubMed search for related case-report literature returned zero results. No independent primary source (trial registry detail, published case report, or sponsor statement) was located this session to corroborate causality or rule it out.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

Cause-of-death attribution for the 2006 phase 2 trial subject is stated by FDA's briefing without causal detail; an independent source (trial registry or published safety report) should be sought to confirm or contextualize before publication.

REMEDIATION 2026-08-29: targeted attempt made to resolve the cause-of-death gap. Located the matching ConjuChem Phase 2 trial on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00267527, "CJC 1295 in HIV Patients With Visceral Obesity," terminated September 2006) via the ClinicalTrials.gov API, but its public registry record gives no termination reason or adverse-event/cause-of-death detail. A PubMed search (CJC-1295 DAC death) returned zero results. A tertiary source (Wikipedia) reports an unsourced physician opinion attributing the death to pre-existing coronary disease, but this could not be traced to a primary source this session. Gap remains unresolved; still requires a reviewer with access to the full trial record, sponsor safety report, or FDA adverse-event database.
CAS number and UNII identifiers were not resolved from the fetched PubChem page and require follow-up against a structured database session that can render the full record.

REMEDIATION 2026-08-29: targeted attempt made to resolve CAS/UNII for PubChem CID 91971820. Queried the FDA/NCATS Global Substance Registration System (GSRS) for "CJC-1295"; it returned 8 substance records (multiple CAS/UNII pairs across salt and conjugated forms) with one clear exact-name match (UNII 62RC32V9N7, CAS 446262-90-4), but its reported molecular formula could not be confidently reconciled with either PubChem CID's formula, so the identifier was not written into the packet to avoid an unverified figure. CAS/UNII for CID 91971820 remain unresolved; a reviewer with direct GSRS/PubChem API or database access should confirm the correct salt-form mapping. Separately, the DAC vs. non-DAC identity ambiguity noted alongside this gap WAS resolved this session via a second PubChem record (CID 91976842, "CJC1295 Without DAC").

FDA's bulk-drug-substances nomination/withdrawal status for CJC-1295 is time-volatile (the PCAC briefing and the withdrawn-nominations page may reflect different stages of the same review); reconfirm current status against the live FDA pages at review time.

REMEDIATION 2026-08-29: live FDA bulk-drug-substances page re-fetched and confirms CJC-1295 is still listed under "nominated but withdrawn" as of today; independent legal/regulatory-trade reporting (FDA Law Blog, April 2026) added to the packet, documenting CJC-1295's prior September 2023 placement in FDA's Category 2 interim-policy list and the resulting Evexias/Farmakeio APA lawsuit, for a more complete regulatory timeline.

Human evidence is limited to short-duration pharmacodynamic (GH/IGF-I) trials in healthy adults; no controlled human efficacy or long-term safety data exist for the body-composition, anti-aging, or recovery uses driving current demand.
